_lime_note: lb ground limestone per 100 sq ft to reach pH 6.5. Iowa State columns: sandy loam, loam, clay loam. Our textures map sand->sandy_loam, loam->loam, clay->clay_loam, silt->loam.
_sulfur_note: Ohio State AGF-507, lb elemental S per acre to lower the top 6 inches to pH 6.5 (non-calcareous soils), divided by 435.6 for per 100 sq ft. Columns: sand, silt loam, clay. Our textures map sand->sand, loam/silt->silt_loam, clay->clay. The 6.5 row (0) is added so pH 6.5-7.0 can be interpolated.
lime_how: Use the rate on your lab soil test if you have one; this is a starting estimate.
Check the bag: if the product is weaker than pure ground limestone, more is needed (the label or your extension office can tell you how much).
Spread evenly, then mix into the top few inches by tilling or spading.
Apply 3 to 4 months before planting if the pH needs to rise a lot. Fall is a good time.
For large amounts, split it over two seasons and retest the pH in a year.
Don't over-lime, especially sandy soil low in organic matter: lowering pH again is hard.
sulfur_how: Use elemental (ground) sulfur. Work it into the top few inches.
It works slowly, through soil microbes: expect a few months or longer.
Apply in spring or summer; in fall and winter the soil is too cold for it to work.
Retest the pH before adding more.
Above pH 7.5 the soil may contain free lime (calcareous); then far more sulfur is needed and it is often impractical. Get a lab test first.
safety: Wear gloves, safety glasses and a dust mask when spreading lime or sulfur.
Don't spread on windy days; keep children and pets off until it is worked into the soil.
Store sulfur away from heat or flames, and follow the product label.
